note: An audit of the session-start work found that _store_summary's read-only promise was false. It opened the store through SqliteStore, whose _connect runs `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` on every open (nestor/sqlite_store.py:325) and mkdir(parents=True) on the store's parent -- so a store in SQLite's default `delete` mode was silently converted by the boot check. Measured on a copy of a real demo store forced back to `delete`: sha256 231f6ebabbf25652 -> 14f49f09c1750713, journal mode delete -> wal, and -wal/-shm sidecars left behind. The claim in 0126 and in two docstrings was wrong one layer below where the code was looking, and no test caught it because every fixture built its store with `nestor demo` or memory_init(), both of which set WAL at creation, making the re-open a genuine no-op.

decisions.question: How does a boot probe read a store without writing to it, when SqliteStore cannot be asked for a read?
decisions.commitment: It bypasses SqliteStore and opens a raw `sqlite3.connect('file:<db>?mode=ro', uri=True)`. No read-only door exists on SqliteStore -- the constructor takes only a path, and _connect unconditionally sets WAL and mkdirs the parent -- and adding one is product surface this hook has no business growing on its own. Measured after the change: a `delete`-mode store reads correctly with its bytes and journal mode unchanged and no sidecars created.
decisions.why: The alternative fixes were worse. Adding a read-only mode to SqliteStore is a product change to serve a boot nicety, and would need its own decision. Dropping the counts entirely would keep the promise by giving up the information that makes the line useful -- an empty store and a full one would read the same. Opening read-only is the narrow fix that keeps both the promise and the number.

decisions.question: What is the promise now, stated so it is actually true?
decisions.commitment: The store's own bytes are never modified. That is narrower than the original 'creates nothing': reading a WAL-mode store still creates -wal and -shm sidecars, because SQLite requires shared memory to read that journal mode at all, and the only flag that avoids it (immutable=1) is unsafe on a store somebody may be writing to. The docstrings and 0126 now state the limit rather than a cleanliness the code cannot deliver.
decisions.why: The original defect was not the write -- it was a promise made one abstraction layer above where the write happened, and then repeated in a decision record. Replacing a false absolute with a true bounded claim is the fix for that class of error; replacing it with a different absolute would repeat it. A reader who needs to know whether a boot leaves sidecars can now find out, and a reader who needs to know whether their store is safe gets an answer that holds.

decisions.question: Why did the original tests pass, and what stops that recurring?
decisions.commitment: Every fixture created its store via `nestor demo` or SqliteStore.memory_init(), both of which set WAL at creation -- so re-opening it never changed anything and the assertion was true on the states it was given. test_a_non_wal_store_is_not_rewritten_by_the_probe now forces a store to `delete` mode, strips its sidecars, and requires the sha256 and the journal mode to survive the probe; run against the code as it shipped, it fails on the hash. test_the_read_only_summary_agrees_with_memory_stats pins the hand-written count query against memory.stats so the duplication that reading-without-writing forced cannot drift.
decisions.why: A test whose fixtures only construct the passing state proves the fixtures, not the invariant. The read-only claim covered every store the check might meet, but the suite only ever showed it one kind -- so the coverage gap and the false claim had exactly the same shape, and fixing the code without widening the fixtures would have left the next such defect equally invisible.
